title: Selective Language Damage with Parameter-Decomposition Subcomponents
text:
1 Introduction
Model-editing studies test locality by measuring how well an edit preserves predictions outside its intended scope (Yao et al. 2023, sec. 2). In factual editing, ROME tests this by checking whether editing one subject changes facts about nearby subjects (Meng et al. 2022, sec. 3.3). Related languages provide a similar test for next-token prediction. Zeroing parameters important for Spanish raises Italian and Portuguese perplexity (Zhang et al. 2024, Table 11). Deactivating French neurons also affects Spanish (Tang et al. 2024, sec. 3.3.1). To compare edits on this test, the first requirement is that they change the target by roughly the same amount.
adVersarial Parameter Decomposition (VPD) approximates a model’s weight matrices with sums of rank-one subcomponents. Its training objective rewards approximations that can use few subcomponents on a given input (Bushnaq et al. 2026, sec. 2), following earlier attribution-based and stochastic decompositions (Braun et al. 2025; Bushnaq et al. 2025). The decomposition offers a set of directions in weight space. If a direction contributes more to target-language predictions than to predictions in a related language, scaling that direction may produce a selective edit.1
Bushnaq tested this idea by training scalar coefficients of selected VPD subcomponents to suppress German (Bushnaq 2026). An edit to one subcomponent chosen by its interpretation label (layer 3 attention value, index 513) damaged German with little change in English, French or Spanish. Italian prediction worsened too.
A numerical rule selects one subcomponent per target using target and English text. German, Spanish and French are the targets of deliberate damage, and Dutch, Portuguese and Italian, respectively, probe the collateral effects. The figures and tables call this second language in each pair protected. None of the methods uses it as a selection or training input for these runs. The comparison includes rank-one LoRA, full-matrix fine-tuning and neuron edits. Each method is calibrated to raise target cross-entropy by 0.5 or 1 nat/token on validation text. Measuring loss in both languages on new Europarl session text shows how much target damage each edit achieves and how much carries over to the related language (Koehn 2005).

title: Selective Language Damage with Parameter-Decomposition Subcomponents
text:
2 Methods

2.1 Model and data
The base model \(W_0\) is Goodfire’s four-layer, 67M-parameter decoder-only language model, trained on a subset of the Pile (Bushnaq et al. 2026, sec. 3.1; Gao et al. 2020). Its VPD dictionary contains 38,912 rank-one subcomponents across 24 matrices.
Damage is the increase in mean next-token cross-entropy (CE) from \(W_0\), in nat/token. Each Europarl date supplies one window per language starting at the same aligned speaker turn. I repeat selection and training on three overlapping target subsets (draws), with different seeds for the learned updates. All draws share 256 English windows from Europarl, WikiText-2 (Merity et al. 2017) and the Pile. The subcomponent selector uses 256 further English windows to check shortlist curvature. Calibration uses separate validation windows. Evaluation covers 64 development dates and 58 confirmation dates (Appendix A).


2.2 Subcomponent selection
A subcomponent \(A_c=u_cv_c^\top\) reads the scalar \(v_c^\top x\) from the input \(x\) and writes \(u_c(v_c^\top x)\) to the output. A coefficient change edits the size or sign of that contribution while keeping both directions fixed. In the original matrix \(W_m\), the coefficient is 1. Changing it to \(1+\alpha\) gives \[W_m'=(W_m-A_c)+(1+\alpha)A_c=W_m+\alpha A_c.\] The term \(W_m-A_c\) contains the other subcomponents and the decomposition residual. A coefficient of zero removes \(A_c\), and a negative coefficient reverses its contribution. The subcomponent keeps its original norm, so the weight change has Frobenius norm \(|\alpha|\,\lVert A_c\rVert_F\).
Let \(g_c\) be the derivative at \(\alpha=0\) of mean target CE along \(A_c\). A small edit changes target CE by approximately \(\alpha g_c\). On English text, the corresponding KL from the base model is approximately \(\tfrac12q_c\alpha^2\), where \(q_c\) estimates directional Fisher curvature. For a fixed small target CE increase \(\delta\), this gives an English KL cost of about \(\tfrac12q_c(\delta/g_c)^2\). The resulting ranking score is \[\frac{g_c^2}{q_c+\varepsilon\lVert A_c\rVert_F^2},\] where the floor \(\varepsilon\lVert A_c\rVert_F^2\) limits the influence of small curvature estimates. Appendix A gives the curvature estimator and shortlist procedure.
The local score supplies the search order. Actual target CE at finite coefficients determines the final choice. On the target training windows, the search tests \(\alpha=\operatorname{sign}(g_c)\,a\) at increasing doses \(a\) up to 2. It selects the first shortlisted direction that reaches 1 nat/token of damage, or the first to reach 0.5 if none reaches 1. A shortlist that reaches neither threshold yields no edit.


2.3 Comparison methods

Rank-one LoRA (Hu et al. 2022) matches the selected edits’ rank and location. It learns both factors of a rank-one update to layer 0’s attention output matrix, which contains all three selected subcomponents.
Full-matrix fine-tuning learns an unrestricted update across all 24 weight matrices.
Neuron edits select the top \(k\) MLP neurons by their excess activation frequency on target text over English, then reduce their output weights. Both \(k\) and the scale are calibrated to the target effect (Tang et al. 2024; Kojima et al. 2024).
Randomized-dictionary edits apply the subcomponent selection rule after independent random signed permutations of the dictionary’s input and output coordinates in each matrix. This preserves subcomponent norms and pairwise angles within each matrix while changing their alignment with the model’s weights. If this search reaches the required target effect, it can test selectivity after disrupting that alignment.

Both learned methods train for 200 steps per draw. Their loss adds a per-window hinge penalty for target CE rises below 1 nat/token to English KL divergence from the base model, with weight 1 on KL. The resulting update can then be scaled down during calibration.


2.4 Matching target effects
Calibration adjusts each edit’s strength on target validation text. An edit is matched if its mean CE rise falls within 0.02 nat/token of \(\tau\), where \(\tau\) is 0.5 or 1 nat/token. The calibrated coefficients stay fixed on evaluation text. The results give both the achieved target effect and the effect on the related language. The prespecified evaluation tolerance for each edit in the main comparison is \(\tau\pm0.1\) nat/token.
Within each target, all three draws gave the same VPD subcomponent and the same calibrated dose at each \(\tau\). This yielded six distinct edits. Each reduced the coefficient from 1 to \(1-a\). Three coefficients stayed above zero and three crossed zero, two only slightly (Table 2).


2.5 Evaluation
The related languages were absent from the selection and training inputs for these runs. In earlier work I had used related-language development text and identified the German subcomponent with Dutch in view. I fixed the edits, comparators and main analysis before the 64-date development readout and evaluated the same edits once on the 58 further dates. Appendix A.3 gives the chronology and prior access.

An edit was eligible only if the CE rise was at most 0.1 nat/token on each English check. For each language pair, \(\tau\) and comparator, the estimate averages the difference in related-language CE rise first across eligible matched draws and then across session dates. Resampling dates gives simultaneous 95% intervals for variation over text with the edits and training runs held fixed. Appendix A.2 describes the comparison families and English checks.

text:
3 Results

3.1 Related-language damage
All matched edits in the main comparison passed the English eligibility checks and stayed within the prespecified target-effect tolerance on the 58 new dates. Figure 1 shows the achieved effects in both languages. The six VPD edits raised related-language CE by 0.0003–0.0053 nat/token, compared with 0.027–0.236 for rank-one LoRA, 0.058–0.407 for full-matrix fine-tuning and 0.423–0.876 for neuron edits. These ranges span individual edits across both calibration levels and all three language pairs (Table 1).






Figure 1: Achieved target and protected-language CE rises on 58 confirmation dates. Each VPD point is one fixed subcomponent edit shared by three draws. Each comparator has one edit per draw, and points can overlap. The shaded bands show the prespecified target tolerance of \(\tau\pm0.1\) nat/token. The vertical axis is logarithmic to resolve small protected-language effects.




All 18 estimable main contrasts have simultaneous 95% intervals below zero (Figure 2, top row). For example, at \(\tau=1\) the German VPD edit raised Dutch CE by 0.089 nat/token less than the mean over the three rank-one LoRA draws. The interval for VPD minus LoRA is [−0.100, −0.077] nat/token. Each of the six VPD edits enters three contrasts. The six planned randomized-dictionary contrasts lack estimates because that search produced no matched edit. Exact estimates are in Appendix B.

A post hoc analysis also found smaller changes in related-language predictions by KL divergence from the base model, with all 18 intervals for VPD minus comparator below zero.


3.2 Achieved target effects
Two edits can meet the target tolerance and still differ in achieved damage. In a post hoc comparison on the new dates, 15 of 18 simultaneous intervals for VPD minus comparator fall entirely within ±0.1 nat/token (Figure 2, bottom row). All three exceptions are at \(\tau=1\). Their means are positive and their upper bounds exceed +0.1, with one interval extending below zero. This pattern gives little support to systematically smaller target effects as an explanation for the VPD result.






Figure 2: Differences in CE rise (VPD minus comparator) with simultaneous 95% intervals. The top row compares related-language damage and uses a different horizontal scale for each comparator. Values below zero indicate less damage from VPD. The bottom row compares achieved target effects in a separate post hoc analysis and uses a common horizontal scale. The shaded band marks the post hoc agreement criterion of ±0.1 nat/token. Filled markers show confirmation on 58 dates. Open markers show development on 64 dates.



A post hoc check of the 58 confirmation windows found that each fixed VPD edit raised target CE on every window. The six largest increases accounted for 13–14% of each edit’s summed target CE increase. Related-language CE rose on 30–47 windows per edit. The six largest increases accounted for 30–43% of the sum of positive related-language changes. The largest such increase on a single window was 0.037 nat/token.


3.3 Preservation of English predictions
The English CE check measures the change in loss on the observed next tokens. A post hoc comparison uses \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{W_0}\,\|\,p_{\mathrm{edit}})\) to measure the change across the full prediction distributions. Both learned methods had lower English KL than the VPD edits in all 18 comparisons across targets, draws and \(\tau\) on the new dates. On four English sets from validation and development, LoRA had lower KL in 72 of 72 comparisons and full-matrix fine-tuning in 65 of 72. These are descriptive counts that reuse both edits and text sets.
The VPD edits’ mean English KL was below 10⁻³ nat/token on the new dates (Table 1). Their Frobenius weight-change norms were larger than the learned edits’. The trade-off depends on which language is measured. The learned objectives penalize English KL directly, and the test of related-language damage uses languages outside those objectives.

3.4 Expanded training comparison
The 200-step learned runs selected the highest learning rate tested for LoRA and the lowest for full-matrix fine-tuning. Either grid could have missed a better setting. I tested an expanded training recipe on the previously evaluated development dates. It used 2,000 steps, a larger hinge margin, wider learning-rate grids and three seeds per draw, with the same validation calibration targets.
Compared with the original recipe on those dates, the expanded recipe reduced related-language CE rise for full-matrix fine-tuning in six of six target–\(\tau\) combinations and for LoRA in five of six. The VPD edits still caused less related-language damage. Across the learned methods and both calibration levels, mean achieved target effects differed from VPD by at most 0.07 nat/token. The expanded recipe changed several settings together and the runs’ convergence remains unestablished. Appendix A.1 gives the exploratory analysis and training diagnostics.

title: Selective Language Damage with Parameter-Decomposition Subcomponents
text:
4 Discussion

4.1 Choice within the VPD dictionary
Using the same dictionary with different rules tests how much the choice of subcomponent matters. Two alternative rules selected the subcomponent most aligned with a learned update. A third ranked subcomponents by the target-minus-English difference in VPD’s learned causal-importance scores, which set lower bounds on subcomponent coefficients during decomposition training. Each rule caused at least as much related-language damage as the main selector wherever estimates were available. For the causal-importance rule, the additional CE rise was 0.48–1.37 nat/token on the new dates at similar target effects. Reusing the previously chosen German subcomponent produced the same edits as the main selector. These comparisons are descriptive and some use fewer than three draws. Appendix A.1 describes the rules and which draws are eligible.
I also checked Bushnaq’s direction (layer 3 attention value, index 513) in a post hoc shortlist scan. At a German validation target of 0.5 nat/token, it raised Dutch CE on the 64 development dates by 0.0012 nat/token, compared with 0.0036 for the direction selected here (layer 0 attention output, index 268). Each direction gave the same calibrated edit across all three draws. The 513 readout covers Dutch CE. Achieved German test damage, English eligibility and Italian damage remain unmeasured in that comparison.


4.2 Contribution of the dictionary
The randomized-dictionary control tested whether the same search could find a comparably selective direction after changing the dictionary’s alignment with the weights. Across all nine target–draw combinations, no shortlisted direction reached even 0.5 nat/token of target CE rise within the dose limit of 2. Selectivity at the required effect therefore remains unmeasured for the randomized directions.
Two exploratory comparisons used directions outside the dictionary on development text. A whitened rank-one selector used the target gradient and an approximate English Fisher curvature. Its calibrated edits caused more related-language damage than the VPD edits. It used the selected VPD subcomponent’s norm and the main selector’s curvature floor, which limits attribution to the choice of dictionary. Applying the main selector to the weight matrices’ singular components yielded no eligible comparison. Every singular-component edit that reached \(\tau\) exceeded the English CE limit. The decomposition’s contribution remains open.


4.3 Scope of the comparison

The confirmation tests six fixed edits on new parliamentary text in one model. The previously viewed development text and the earlier choice of the German subcomponent limit what can be attributed to the selection rule (Section 2.5). The results leave open how the rule performs on new tasks, models or languages, and whether the selected directions implement a language-specific mechanism.
English was the only language the learned objectives explicitly protected. Giving those objectives related-language examples could change the comparison. The calibration matches means, so edits with similar achieved target damage can still distribute that damage differently across windows. The main result concerns collateral damage under this matching criterion. For the six fixed edits, the VPD directions spared the related languages better than the tested comparators, while the learned updates better preserved English predictions.


Code and data. The study guide explains how to replay the analysis from per-date measurements, including the window-level check and the archived German shortlist comparison. A model rerun of the confirmation would require the unpublished text windows.

AI assistance. I used OpenAI Codex and Anthropic Claude for research planning, code development, data analysis and manuscript preparation. Scientific Agent Skills (Kassis et al. 2026) supplied the scientific-writing, scientific-critical-thinking, peer-review and citation-management workflows used to review organization, claims and references.

title: Selective Language Damage with Parameter-Decomposition Subcomponents
text:
Appendix A — Method details
Data. Europarl v7 (Koehn 2005) supplies one 257-token window per session date (256 predictions). Windows start at the same aligned speaker turn in each language, but each language is tokenized and truncated independently, so the windows need not cover identical content. Each target has three draws of 64 of its 128 training windows and 32 validation windows for calibration. The English validation set has 64 windows: 32 Europarl and 32 English-filtered Pile. The retain pool has 256 windows: 128 Europarl English training, 64 WikiText-2 validation and 64 English-filtered Pile validation.
Selection. The model Fisher estimate \(q_c\) averages squared directional scores using eight model-sampled label sets per retain window (Martens 2020; Kunstner et al. 2019). The floor \(\varepsilon\) is the 1st percentile of \(q_c / \lVert A_c\rVert_F^2\). The top 64 subcomponents are re-ranked using the larger of \(q_c\) and a second estimate on 256 other English windows, before the dose search of Section 2.2. Curvature checks passed on the NVIDIA L40S used for the original runs, but the batch-splitting check failed on the tested A10 and L4. Verified selector reruns cover only the German target’s first draw on the L40S, with the VPD dictionary and one randomized dictionary. GPU-dependent Fisher-label sampling can change selections on other hardware.
Calibration. The first dose-grid crossing of τ is bracketed, then bisected for at most five steps until within the matching tolerance. Neuron edits scale the top \(k\) neurons’ output weights by \(1-f\): calibration takes the smallest power-of-two \(k\) from 1 to 256 whose full removal reaches τ, then calibrates \(f\). Randomized dictionaries use a separate seed per draw.
Learned updates. The 200-step updates use Adam (Kingma and Ba 2015), 10 warm-up steps, gradient clipping at 1.0, and 8 target and 8 English windows per step. Calibration scales the final update \(D\) to \(\beta D\), with \(\beta \le 1\). The learning rate is chosen once per target on draw 0, by the lowest English validation KL at τ = 1. Every target chose 3e-3 for LoRA and 1e-6 for full-matrix fine-tuning, respectively the upper and lower edges of the tested grids.

A.1 Alternative selectors and extended training
Two within-dictionary alternatives use the first step of orthogonal matching pursuit (Pati et al. 1993; Mallat and Zhang 1993): they normalize each subcomponent to unit Frobenius norm, select the one with the largest absolute inner product with a learned update, and use that inner product’s sign. One uses full-matrix fine-tuning; the other uses rank-one LoRA across all 24 matrices. VPD’s learned causal-importance score sets the lower bound on a subcomponent’s mask during decomposition training. A third rule selects the largest mean target-minus-English score with a negative sign, adapting Bushnaq’s top-16 ranking to one subcomponent (Bushnaq 2026). The fourth alternative reuses the previously chosen German subcomponent. All use the main calibration rule. Some fail to reach τ or lack an eligible learned checkpoint; their contrasts include only the available matched, usable draws and use a separate simultaneous family.
The extended learned updates use 2,000 steps, a hinge margin of 1.5, wider learning-rate grids and three seeds per draw. The whitened selector maximizes the squared target gradient relative to damped K-FAC curvature on English text (Martens and Grosse 2015), then tests doses from 1/64 to 8. The SVD control applies the main selection rule unchanged to the singular components of all 24 weight matrices; these reconstruct the weights exactly, whereas VPD leaves a residual.
Extended contrasts compare unpaired means over each method’s matched, usable runs. A sensitivity analysis excludes 7 of 27 LoRA runs whose English validation KL at step 2,000 exceeded twice their minimum from step 100 onward. Both analyses favor the subcomponent edits. Training diagnostics did not establish objective convergence and were not used to select edits.
These exploratory comparisons were specified before the runs. Analysis rules were fixed before readout, after selection outcomes and target and English validation effects were known. This chronology comes from the author’s records, without independent timestamps.


A.2 Evaluation and intervals
Evaluation sets. Development uses 64 session dates. English eligibility checks use Europarl test text (64 windows), WikiText-2 test text (32) and Pile test documents (512). Confirmation uses 58 further dates (48 main and 10 reserve, analyzed together), including English. An edit must pass both development and confirmatory English checks to enter a confirmatory comparison.
Main comparisons. The planned family contains four comparators × three language pairs × two values of τ. Each contrast is the subcomponent edit’s CE rise minus the comparator’s, averaged over matched, eligible draws and then over dates. Simultaneous 95% intervals use 2,000 shared bootstrap resamples of session dates (Efron 1979) and a max-|t| critical value (Montiel Olea and Plagborg-Møller 2019, supplement, Algorithm 3). Training draws and seeds, selected subcomponents, language pairs and the model remain fixed. The randomized-dictionary contrasts have no estimates because the control produced no feasible edits.
Target-effect checks. The prespecified tolerance for each edit’s target CE rise was τ ± 0.1 nat/token; all edits in the main confirmation comparison met it. The post hoc agreement analysis instead compares the target effects of two methods. Its simultaneous family includes 54 coordinates per readout: target gaps, related-language CE contrasts and related-language KL contrasts, using 20,000 shared date resamples. KL is \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{W_0}\,\|\,p_{\mathrm{edit}})\), averaged over next-token positions.


A.3 Prior data access
The selection, comparison and analysis rules were fixed on 11 October 2026 before the development readout. Later that day, the unchanged edits were evaluated once on 58 further dates under an amendment fixed before those windows were parsed. The chronology relies on the author’s records; there is no independently timestamped preregistration.
In an earlier experiment, I had chosen German subcomponent 0.attn.o:268 with Dutch in view. It was also the top German candidate in a pilot of this selector. Dutch, Portuguese and Italian development text and NTREX Dutch and Italian text (Federmann et al. 2022) had been read or used previously. The development dates therefore do not provide a fresh test. The Pile also contains a European Parliament component (Gao et al. 2020, sec. 2.17); overlap with the model’s pretraining subset is unknown.

title: Transferring Learned Repairs Between Fine-Tunes
text:
1 Introduction
Fine-tuning recipes are often run again as training data change. If a recipe repeatedly harms a capability that the original model had, an extra weight update can try to restore that capability while keeping the intended change. This extra update is the repair. Suppose a repair is available from an earlier fine-tune, the donor. One option is to keep the donor’s directions fixed and learn how strongly to apply them. A second is to start from the donor and continue training the directions. Fitting a new repair shows whether the donor offers an advantage over starting from scratch.
German and Dutch provide separate measures of the intended change and the collateral damage. Fine-tuning deliberately raises prediction loss on German text. It also raises prediction loss on Dutch, which is outside the fine-tuning objective. A successful repair should bring Dutch predictions back toward the base model while keeping the new German predictions. The comparison uses one donor and two target fine-tunes independently trained from Goodfire’s 67M-parameter model (Bushnaq et al. 2026, sec. 3.1). All three use the same objective and selected learning rate, with different seeds and samples from the same Europarl corpus (Koehn 2005).

title: Transferring Learned Repairs Between Fine-Tunes
text:
2 Experimental design

2.1 What the repair changes
Goodfire’s base model is a four-layer decoder-only transformer trained on a subset of the Pile (Gao et al. 2020). Fine-tuning adds \(D_m\) to each of its 24 attention and MLP matrices \(W_m\). A hinge loss raises German cross-entropy (CE), the mean next-token prediction loss. A KL penalty keeps predictions in English, French, Spanish and Italian (the retain languages) close to the base model’s predictions.
A repair adds a rank-one update \(E_m=b_m a_m^{\top}\) on top of \(W_m+D_m\). For an input \(x\), the added output is \(E_m x=b_m(a_m^{\top}x)\). The input vector \(a_m\) extracts one scalar from \(x\), and the output vector \(b_m\) determines the direction of the change. Multiplying the repair by a coefficient \(c_m\) changes its strength and can reverse its sign. Training the factors can also change which inputs the update responds to and where it sends the added output. This parameterization is the same for the donor and targets. It uses ordinary learned rank-one updates of the form introduced by LoRA (Hu et al. 2022).
I fit the donor repair once on 73,728 prediction positions. For each target, the fixed donor repair applies it without fitting, scaling it down if needed to satisfy the target norm cap. The same capped repair initializes scalar-only fitting, donor initialization and its output-only variant. The last two train one or both vectors as specified in Table 1. All repairs share the constraint \(\lVert E\rVert_F\le\lVert D\rVert_F\), where each norm combines all 24 matrices. The fixed-direction constraint therefore changes the set of available updates within a common rank and norm cap.



Table 1: Repair families. Each update has rank at most one per matrix. Random initialization replaces both donor vectors with Gaussian directions of the same lengths, then applies the same cap. In fresh fitting, \(b_m=0\) and \(a_m\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1/d_{\text{in}})\) as in LoRA.

Fresh fitting and donor initialization train the same parameters. The first fresh seed uses the same initial input vectors that were used to train the donor repair. Its contrast with donor initialization measures the benefit of the fitted donor start as a whole. The norm-matched random start checks whether a nonzero start of the same size is enough. The output-only variant asks how much of the scalar shortfall can be closed while keeping the donor’s input vectors fixed. The comparison includes a second fresh seed and a second random seed at 2,048 fit tokens with a 600-step cap.


2.2 How the repairs are fit and compared
Fitting minimizes the sum of three token-mean KL divergences \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{\text{teacher}}\,\|\,p_{\text{repair}})\) with equal weight. The teacher is the base model for Dutch and the fine-tuned model for German and the retain languages. This objective encourages recovery of Dutch predictions and preservation of the fine-tuned behavior on the other languages. The primary outcome is measured on text using Dutch CE recovery, the fraction of excess prediction loss removed by the repaired model \(X\).
\[
r_{\text{nl}}(X) = 1 - \frac{\mathrm{CE}_{\text{nl}}(X) - \mathrm{CE}_{\text{nl}}(\text{base})}{\mathrm{CE}_{\text{nl}}(\text{fine-tuned}) - \mathrm{CE}_{\text{nl}}(\text{base})}.
\]
Recovery of 0% leaves Dutch CE at the fine-tuned value. Recovery of 100% brings Dutch CE to the base-model value. Differences in recovery are in percentage points (pp).
Each target repair is fit at 256, 512 or 2,048 unique prediction positions (fit tokens). Larger budgets contain the smaller budgets’ positions. Ordinary runs use full-batch Adam at four learning rates per family and save checkpoints every 50 steps. At each step cap (50, 100, 200 or 600), checkpoints saved through that step are eligible for selection. The chosen checkpoint can be earlier than the cap. The full budget is 2,048 fit tokens with a 600-step cap for ordinary runs.
Fitting, checkpoint selection and final evaluation use separate text. The two targets share the windows at each stage. On 32 selection dates, checkpoints that preserve German behavior and move Dutch predictions toward the base model qualify for ranking by Dutch recovery. A retain-language guard determines which ranked checkpoint can be selected. The target readout measures recovery and rechecks those constraints for the selected checkpoints on 92 further session dates. One joint bootstrap over dates (Efron 1979) gives paired 95% percentile intervals within each target. Appendix A gives the selection rule, including the handling of ties.


2.3 The primary test of fixed directions
The primary comparison pits donor-initialized fitting against scalar-only fitting at 2,048 tokens. The two start at the same repair, so their main difference is which updates they can learn. To give the scalar fit more opportunity to find a good solution, I extend its usual four learning-rate runs with two full-batch projected-gradient runs. The expanded scalar search pools the two final candidates with 48 ordinary checkpoints. The two repair families thus have unequal optimization budgets in this comparison.
The comparison is interpretable only if the fine-tune causes measurable Dutch damage, both selected repairs pass the readout constraints and both additional scalar runs meet the declared stopping criteria (assessability and optimizer checks). The prespecified primary margin is 3 pp. A paired interval wholly above that margin establishes an advantage greater than 3 pp for this comparison. An interval wholly below it excludes such an advantage, and an interval touching or crossing it leaves the decision open. Other contrasts use descriptive intervals without multiplicity correction. Five predefined secondary contrasts assess equivalence by checking whether the interval lies inside ±2 pp. The study protocol fixed both margins without a stated derivation.

3 Results

3.1 Rescaling the fixed directions leaves more Dutch damage
Before fitting a repair, the fine-tunes raise Dutch CE by 0.187 and 0.189 nat/token on the primary and replication targets. Applying the capped donor repair with no target fitting recovers 86.3% of that damage on the primary target and 58.6% on replication. With ordinary fitting and a 600-step cap, donor initialization and fresh fitting clear 95% recovery at all three token budgets on both targets, while the scalar-only repairs stay below 90% (Figure 1).

Training only the output vectors closes most of the gap at the full budget. It adds 10.2 pp and 19.1 pp over the expanded scalar search on the two targets. Training both vectors adds a further 1.1 pp and 1.3 pp (Table 7). The output-only run inherits the donor’s input vectors and its trained output vectors, so this comparison leaves the contribution of the input directions unresolved.


3.2 Donor initialization helps most in short, low-data runs
When the fitting budget is small, starting from the donor can get to higher recovery under the same step cap. With 256 fit tokens and a 50-step cap, it leads the first fresh seed by 4.4 pp on the primary target and 4.1 pp on replication. It leads the first norm-matched random start by 4.9 pp and 4.5 pp. At this same budget, keeping the donor input vectors fixed and training only the outputs leads fresh fitting by 4.2 and 4.1 pp. Thus most of the observed early gain is present with half as many trainable parameters. The size of the advantage varies across budgets and step caps (Figure 2). The small-budget comparisons use one seed per control and a single set of fitting positions shared by both targets.

title: Transferring Learned Repairs Between Fine-Tunes
text:
4 Discussion
Rescaling the donor repair recovered much of the lost Dutch performance. Training its directions recovered more. The donor start offered its clearest advantage over fresh fitting in the short, low-data runs.
Reusing a weight direction while fitting a scale has precedents in task arithmetic and safety repair. Task arithmetic adds or subtracts scaled weight differences (Ilharco et al. 2023). RESTA uses a scaled safety vector (Bhardwaj et al. 2024), and SafeGene fits separate scalars on frozen adapters in selected layers (Wang et al. 2026, sec. 3.5). SPoT illustrates the initialization approach with transferred soft prompts (Vu et al. 2022). This experiment puts the two reuse strategies under a shared rank and norm constraint on repeated fine-tunes from the same recipe.
Bushnaq scaled a German-related component from Goodfire’s adVersarial Parameter Decomposition (VPD) and compared it with LoRA on the same base model (Bushnaq et al. 2026; Bushnaq 2026). Both that edit and the scalar repair studied here keep input and output directions fixed. The VPD component came from a decomposition of the base weights. The donor directions came from fitting a Dutch repair. The shortfall on the fitting text suggests a comparison for a future VPD study. At the same rank and norm budget, how much of the training objective can coefficient edits achieve when an update with trainable directions is available as a reference?

title: Transferring Learned Repairs Between Fine-Tunes
text:
5 Limits of these conclusions
The comparisons are conditional on one donor, one base model, one recipe and two target fine-tunes. Resampling dates measures uncertainty on evaluation text for fixed repairs. Variation across donors, targets, fit windows and short-run initialization seeds would require additional runs. The donor passed its own readiness check before use, so this test describes transfer from a selected, effective repair. To test the input directions themselves, two output-only fits could start with zero output vectors. One would freeze the donor input vectors and the other would freeze random directions of the same lengths. Both would begin with the same zero update. Zhu et al. (2024) studied fitting LoRA outputs with frozen random inputs. The results measure prediction-loss recovery on the tested languages. Transfer of new skills, safety alignment and the internal mechanism of Dutch recovery remain open.

Appendix A — Method details
Fine-tunes. Adam (Kingma and Ba 2015) learns full-matrix additive updates \(D_m\) to each layer’s query, key, value, output and two MLP matrices (24 total), with embeddings and norms frozen. It runs for 200 steps on the per-window hinge \(\max(0, 1 - \Delta\mathrm{CE}_{\text{de}})\) (1-nat margin) plus retain-language KL with weight 1. Checkpoints are selected on German and retain-language validation metrics. The donor used the checkpoint selected from runs at learning rates 3e-6 and 1e-5. Both targets reused the selected rate, 3e-6, and each chose its own checkpoint by the same rule. Before fitting a repair, I required a usable fine-tune that passed validation and raised Dutch CE by at least 0.05 nat/token on the 32 selection dates. Both targets passed (0.174 and 0.188). The separate readout damage criterion applies on the 92 evaluation dates.
Repairs. Ordinary fitting uses Adam. The donor starts fresh (Table 1), using 73,728 prediction positions, three learning rates and 200 minibatch steps per run. Checkpoints saved every 25 steps undergo selection on donor validation windows by the rule below. The selected repair passes a separate donor readiness check, including at least 80% Dutch CE recovery on 112 dates after excluding 16 previously inspected dates. Target repair runs use a 10-step learning-rate warm-up and then a constant rate. They save checkpoints every 50 steps at four learning rates (Table 4), giving 48 candidates per family at the 600-step cap. Donor starts are capped as \(\min(1, \lVert D\rVert_F / \lVert E_{\text{donor}}\rVert_F)\, E_{\text{donor}}\).

The 50-step cap uses the same grid. Several output-only cells and donor-initialized replication at 512 tokens select the first checkpoint at the lowest rate, which can explain repeated values across caps. Advantages over fresh and random starts are nonmonotonic in budget and cap.
Selection. To qualify, a candidate must keep between 90% and 110% of the fine-tune’s German CE damage. Its German prediction distribution must also remain close to the fine-tune’s. Specifically, \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{\text{fine-tuned}}\,\|\,p_{\text{repair}})\) can be at most 5% of \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{\text{fine-tuned}}\,\|\,p_{\text{base}})\) on German text. On Dutch text, the repair must reduce \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{\text{base}}\,\|\,p_{\text{repair}})\) relative to the fine-tuned model. I rank qualifying candidates by Dutch CE recovery, breaking ties by smaller norm and then listing order. Selection takes the first of the top five candidates that keeps any CE increase on each retain language to at most 0.01 nat/token above the fine-tuned model. Readout applies these constraints to the selected repairs.
Data. Fit budgets exclude each window’s initial context token and split predictions 2:1:1 across Dutch, German and retain text. At 256 tokens, one Dutch window contributes 128 predictions, one German 64, and four retain windows 16 each. At 512 tokens these counts double. At 2,048, four Dutch and two German windows contribute 256 each, and one per retain language contributes 128.
The 128 dates available for the donor readiness check later supplied the two disjoint 64-date fine-tuning sets for the targets. The donor’s repair fitting and checkpoint selection used separate sets. The targets’ repair fitting, selection and readout sets used dates outside the donor sets.
Selection and readout use 32 and 92 dates, respectively, with one 257-token window (256 predictions) per language from the same turn. Portuguese, the seventh language, is diagnostic only: its selection windows count toward token and evaluation costs, but not the loss or selection constraints. Readout dates were ineligible if present in recorded project data, pilot or run files, or if their windows duplicated text in use. All passed. Overlap with the base model’s pretraining text remains unknown.
Assessability. The primary contrast requires a Dutch-damage readout interval with lower bound at least 0.025 nat/token. Damage is 0.187 nat/token [0.178, 0.196] on the primary target and 0.189 [0.180, 0.198] on replication. Both selected repairs must satisfy the readout constraints (Table 5), and both additional scalar runs must meet the stopping criteria.
Study record. My records place a dated protocol fixing rules, margins and families before readout-data construction and target fine-tuning. An author-dated amendment fixed readout data and clarified the primary interpretation before any target fine-tune or readout, without changing decision rules. The unpublished protocol, amendment and log lack the independent timestamps needed to verify preregistration.
Uncertainty. Within each target, 5,000 joint date resamples cover all budgets and caps, computing recovery ratios from mean damages. Readout constraints use point estimates over all dates. Equivalence is assessed only for the five contrasts marked in Table 7.

Appendix C — Cost accounting
For each cost measure, let \(C^*\) be a family’s cheapest reaching cost on the tested grid. If the observed per-target difference repeats, reuse repays the donor cost after more than \[
K^* = \frac{C_{\text{donor}}}{C^*(\text{fresh}) - C^*(\text{donor initialization})}
\] targets (Table 3). The donor’s 3,686,400 presentations give \(K^* \approx 10.3\) on each target. All scalar-only settings and both fixed donor repairs fall short of the reference. A random start saves no presentations on the primary target. On replication it gives \(K^* = 18\), charged with the full donor cost although it uses only the lengths of the donor factors.
Unique tokens count fit tokens plus 57,344 selection positions (32 dates × 7 languages × 256). Presentations count fit tokens × optimizer steps across all four learning rates up to the cap, excluding selection forward passes. GPU seconds combine training time prorated to the cap and selection-evaluation time allocated by candidate count. For the expanded scalar search, presentations and GPU seconds also include both additional runs and evaluation of the 48 checkpoints used to choose the second start. The target costs exclude all final readout passes, the pre-fitting damage check and exploration of other settings.
The donor costs 131,072 unique tokens (73,728 fit plus selection), 3,686,400 presentations (3 learning rates × 200 steps × 6,144 tokens per minibatch), and an estimated 336 GPU seconds for training, selection and readout. Its fine-tune is excluded because the donor model is assumed to exist.
The first fresh seed is the reference (Section 3.3), with self-comparison interval [0, 0]. At 256 tokens and a 600-step cap, fresh fitting’s lower bounds, −1.985 pp (primary) and −1.957 pp (replication), narrowly exceed −2 pp and set its lowest unique-token cost.
Sensitivity to the reference and margin (post hoc). I kept the candidate grid, including its first-seed fresh fits, fixed. With the second full-budget fresh seed as the reference and the original 2 pp margin, both targets still reached with 51,200 donor presentations. Fresh fitting now needed 819,200. Its cheapest qualifying budget rose to 2,048 unique fit tokens, compared with 256 for the donor. Changing only the margin also mattered. With the first reference and margins of 1, 2 and 3 pp, the projected first target count with net presentation savings was 5, 11 and 25, respectively. These are alternative readings of the same measured grid. The second fresh seed was available only at full budget.

title: Some Studies of Language Model Weight Edits
text:
Some Studies of Language Model Weight Edits
  I tested how weight edits affect predictions across languages and whether a correction learned for one fine-tune can help another.
  First published 14 October 2026 · Updated 18 November 2026



  
    Selective language editing
    I edit the model’s weights to deliberately worsen its predictions in one language, then check how much a close relative is affected. Across German–Dutch, Spanish–Portuguese and French–Italian, editing one weight subcomponent caused less damage to the related language than rank-one LoRA, full-matrix fine-tuning or neuron edits calibrated for the same amount of target-language damage on validation text. title: Repair transfer
text:
Training the repair
The earlier fine-tune is the donor. The primary target and replication target are two more fine-tunes trained independently from the same base model with the same recipe, different seeds and text sampled from the same distribution (Europarl, a corpus of European Parliament proceedings). I learn one donor repair and reuse it for both targets.
Each repair freezes the fine-tuned weights and adds a rank-one update \(E=ba^\top\) to each of 24 weight matrices. On an input \(x\), the input vector \(a\) reads out a scalar \(a^\top x\) and the output vector \(b\) sets the direction of the added output \(Ex=b(a^\top x)\). Training rewards matching the base model’s Dutch predictions and keeping the fine-tuned model’s predictions in the other five languages.
I compare three ways to fit the repair.

Scalar-only fitting learns one multiplier per matrix. It can amplify, weaken or reverse the donor’s correction along the same direction.
Donor initialization trains both vectors from their donor values. It can change what the correction reads from the input and where it sends the result.
Fresh initialization starts with a zero update and trains both vectors using the target. This provides a baseline for how much the donor helps when both vectors can change.

title: Selective language editing
text:
Edit one rank-one subcomponent
Goodfire’s adVersarial Parameter Decomposition (VPD) breaks a weight matrix \(W\) into a sum of rank-one subcomponents and a residual. The decomposition is trained so that a small number of subcomponents can approximate the model’s computation for a given input. Each subcomponent \(A\) is the outer product of an output vector \(u_{\mathrm{out}}\) and an input vector \(v_{\mathrm{in}}\).
\[
A = u_{\mathrm{out}}v_{\mathrm{in}}^\top.
\]
For an input \(x\), the input vector reads out one number, \(v_{\mathrm{in}}^\top x\). The output vector determines the direction of the resulting contribution to the output.
\[
Ax = u_{\mathrm{out}}\bigl(v_{\mathrm{in}}^\top x\bigr).
\]
I rank subcomponents by how much changing their coefficients is expected to raise target-language loss relative to its effect on English predictions. I then test the highest-ranked candidates on target training text to find one that can cause enough damage.
The edit changes one number, the selected subcomponent’s coefficient \(c\).
\[
W_{\mathrm{edited}} = (W-A) + cA.
\]
The coefficient scales the same rank-one matrix, changing many weights at once. At \(c=1\), the edit reconstructs the original matrix. At \(c=0\), it removes the selected contribution, and at \(c<0\), it reverses its sign.

title: Selective language editing
section: Comparing ways to change the weights
text:
Comparing ways to change the weights
I compare the VPD edit with three other weight edits aimed at worsening target-language predictions while preserving English.

Rank-one LoRA learns its own input and output vectors. Its update has the same rank as the VPD subcomponent and acts on the same weight matrix.
Full-matrix fine-tuning can change every entry of the model’s 24 attention and feed-forward weight matrices.
Neuron edits scale the output weights of neurons selected because they activate more frequently on the target language than on English.

LoRA and full-matrix fine-tuning explicitly penalize changes to English predictions during training.

title: Selective language editing
text:
Matching the intended damage
An edit might spare Dutch simply by barely affecting German. To compare side effects at similar target damage, I adjust each edit’s strength on target-language validation text. The two calibration levels are increases of 0.5 or 1 nat/token in average next-token prediction loss (cross-entropy) relative to the original model. The loss averages the negative log probability assigned to each observed next token.
Using Europarl v7, a corpus of European Parliament proceedings, I then measure the effects of the fixed edits on text from 58 further session dates. Dutch, Portuguese and Italian were excluded from selection and training in this study. Earlier experiments had used development text in these languages and identified the same German subcomponent with Dutch in view. Data and prior access
